newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh cellular phone firm targets villages.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh cellular phone firm targets villages.

text.p: A private cellular telecom venture is targeting the villages of impoverished Bangladesh, home to 75 percent of the country's population, with the aim of ending a monopoly in the nation's mobile phone business.
"Everybody should have the right to own a cellular phone in this country now," Ashraful Huq Chowdhury, project director of Grameen Phone Consortium, said on Wednesday.
Grameen is one of the three local firms awarded contracts for the installation of cellular networks, ending the monopoly of Pacific Bangladesh Telecom Ltd.
"It's a basic requirement of the people in modern world," Chowdhury told Reuters.
Grameen is a subsidiary of Grameen Bank which was set up in 1976 and turned into a fully fledged bank in 1983.

Since then the bank has expanded to 1,056 branches in 36,000 villages and has revolutionised small credit system for rural poor, disbursing 59.6 billion taka ($1.4 billion) to more than two million people.

Chowdhury said Grameen Phone Consortium, with a 34.5 percent share, had formed a venture with Norwegian Telenor International AS (51 percent), Japan's Marubeni Corp and the Washington-based Gonofone Development.
He said the venture would spend $25 million in the first 18 months, which might be increased to more than $65 million in phases.
Pacific Bangladesh officials said little more than 4,000 people in the capital Dhaka had cellular phones.
Chowdhury said the consortium's first target was to install at least one cellular phone in each of the 68,000 villages. The task will begin at the end of the month.

A company statement on Wednesday said the "aim is to serve all people of Bangladesh irrespective of their location or economic conditions". Grameen Bank will allow customers to borrow money to buy cellular phones, the statement added.
Chowdhury said the consortium was contacting cellular phone suppliers such as Swedish LM Ericsson AB, French Alcatel Alsthom and the Finnish Nokia Oy for equipment.
The price of each set would be between 8,000 taka ($200) and 16,000 taka. "It should not exceed 16,000 taka. Maybe it will be less than 8,000 taka," he said. Per capita income is about $260 a year.
The call charge per minute would be one taka in the villages and five taka in towns.
Pacific Bangladesh Telecom is now selling sets at between 37,000 taka and 60,000 taka and charging calls at seven taka per minute.
The other two new Bangladeshi companies that have been allowed to set up cellular networks in the country are Seba Telecom Ltd and IM International.
Telecommunication Ministry officials said the decision to give licences to the cellular phone companies was taken to help create a competitive market.
"This will improve the quality of the service and reduce cost," one official said.
